newsitem.title: USA: Continental pilots say far from labor deal.
newsitem.headline: Continental pilots say far from labor deal.

text.p: Continental Airlines Inc and its pilots will seek federal mediation since the two sides remain far from a compromise on a new labor contract, the union said.
"We're as far apart as you can get. We were so far apart from the company's offer that we decided it was best to go to mediation," said Leonard Nikolai, president of the pilot's union.

The two sides have reached tentative agreements on a number of issues such as seniority, training and physical examinations. But little progress has been made on critical issues such as wages and benefits, the union said.
The pilots are seeking a wage increase of up to 38 percent and improved benefits. Continental offered a counter proposal to the pilots this week.
"We would have expected a low ball proposal on opening day as an opener. But 45 days in to it, they gave us a proposal that was basically an opener," Nikolai said.
The two sides opened contract talks on April 2.

The International Association of Continental Pilots, which represents 4,900 pilots at Continental Airlines and 1,000 pilots at the sister, regional carrier Continental Express, said it is does not expect a new contract agreement to be finalized before June 30, when the current contract becomes amendable.

"I don't think it is achievable. We're willing to put in all the resources needed for the negotiation process, but the date of the contract is not as important as getting a contract with quality," Nikolai said.

After the company's annual shareholders meeting In Houston on Friday, Continental chairman Gordon Bethune said contract talks with the carrier's pilots were going well and that he expected to have a new pact by July 1.
Bethune said bringing in a mediator did not signal problems in the talks. Rather, Continental management generally favors using a mediator to keep negotiations from bogging down, he said.
"We used a mediator from the outset in our (successful) negotiations with flight attendants (last year)," he said.
Labor experts said it was prudent for the two sides to seek mediation instead of getting bogged down in counter-proposals that would only raise frustration levels.

"Mediation gives both parties a nice, friendly atmosphere in which to negotiate without getting into batting comments back and forth in the media," said Joseph Blasi, a professor at Rutgers University's School of Management and Labor Relations.

Lawyers for both sides will meet Monday to outline the logistics of the mediation process. Some negotiations could resume in about two weeks, but formal negotiations with a mediator will not begin for another month or two, Nikolai said.
